{"id": "17:78/q31", "question": "Which prayer is the 'middle prayer' in the related verse?", "turns_on": "The reports identify different prayers as the middle prayer of 2:238.", "positions": [{"id": "17:78/q31/p1", "position": "Fajr, between night and day prayers.", "reasons": "ʿAli and Ubayy say it lies between the prayer sets and is vulnerable to sleep; Jishumi's report adds that it is entered in both angel registers."}, {"id": "17:78/q31/p2", "position": "ʿAṣr.", "reasons": "Abu Hurayra identifies ʿAṣr as the middle prayer; Qashani applies the identification inwardly to the spirit's witnessing."}]}
{"id": "17:85/q01", "question": "Who asked the Prophet about the spirit, and how did the question arise?", "turns_on": "Reports place the question among Jews in Medina or Quraysh in Mecca after consultation with Jews; one names Abu Jahl.", "positions": [{"id": "17:85/q01/p1", "position": "Quraysh asked after Jews suggested a test.", "reasons": "Reports name Nadr ibn al-Harith and Uqba ibn Abi Muayt as envoys; Bursevi also names Ubayy ibn Khalaf. Jewish scholars suggested the Cave youths, Dhul-Qarnayn, and spirit; answering the first two while leaving the third obscure would attest prophethood in some accounts. Ibn Ashur distinguishes a spirit-only consultation and notes Meccan–Yathrib ties. Ibn Abbas's broader account places Quraysh leaders at the Kaaba, accusing Muhammad of dividing society and offering wealth, rule, or treatment."}, {"id": "17:85/q01/p2", "position": "Jews directly questioned him in Medina.", "reasons": "Ibn Masud places the exchange in a field, garden, ruined district, street, or date grove; the Prophet paused, sometimes leaning on a staff or palm stalk, before reciting the revelation. Some Jews warned against asking, regretted asking, or said the answer matched their scripture. Wāḥidī notes Bukhari and Muslim transmit the report. Jishumi says Jewish questioners are one option; al-Zajjaj instead names polytheists."}, {"id": "17:85/q01/p3", "position": "The question concerned Abu Jahl and his companions.", "reasons": "Muqatil names Abu Jahl's party as the occasion."}]}
{"id": "17:85/q02", "question": "How long did revelation pause after the test question?", "turns_on": "The reports give three, twelve, fifteen, or forty days or nights.", "positions": [{"id": "17:85/q02/p1", "position": "Forty days.", "reasons": "Wahidi and Razi report forty days and connect 18:23–24 with the omission of the exception; Baghawi attributes forty to Ikrima."}, {"id": "17:85/q02/p2", "position": "Fifteen days or nights.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya and Biqai connect the delay to the Prophet's promise to answer without saying 'if God wills'; Baghawi records a fifteen-day report."}, {"id": "17:85/q02/p3", "position": "Twelve nights.", "reasons": "Baghawi attributes this to Mujahid; Biqai lists it as a variant."}, {"id": "17:85/q02/p4", "position": "Three days.", "reasons": "Yahya reports Gabriel's delay and his later citation of 19:64: angels descend only by God's command."}]}
{"id": "17:85/q03", "question": "What was the test meant to establish?", "turns_on": "Reports differ in their test formula and Razi disputes whether the proposed test could prove prophethood.", "positions": [{"id": "17:85/q03/p1", "position": "Answering the two historical questions but leaving the spirit unexplained would identify a prophet.", "reasons": "The Jews' scripture allegedly named but did not explain spirit. Wahidi Asbab says answering all or none disqualified him; Abu Hayyan notes variants. Razi objects that stories could be disbelieved and silence proves nothing."}, {"id": "17:85/q03/p2", "position": "The question was an obstinate attempt to embarrass him.", "reasons": "Mawardi compares demands for signs; Jishumi's al-Asamm cites the Jewish book; Burhan and Itqan say the word has many referents, so a general answer defeated the trap. Islahi calls it ridicule."}, {"id": "17:85/q03/p3", "position": "The delayed answer itself showed revelation was from God.", "reasons": "Biqai argues that the Prophet could not compose an answer even while the delay damaged his reputation."}]}
{"id": "17:85/q04", "question": "What did the questioners ask about the spirit?", "turns_on": "The answer can be read against inquiries into essence, origination, Gabriel's descent, or the Quran's source.", "positions": [{"id": "17:85/q04/p1", "position": "They asked what the life-giving spirit is, including its essence, location, and relation to the body.", "reasons": "Jishumi lists its definition, varied perception, and need for life; Wahidi Wajiz gives its reality, manner, and place. Razi says the phrase could also invite questions about substance, spatiality, survival, and happiness. Ibn Ashur says the general phenomenon is known intuitively."}, {"id": "17:85/q04/p2", "position": "They asked whether the spirit is created or eternal.", "reasons": "Mawardi, Tabrisī, Baydawi, Nasafi, Burhan, and Razi report this as a question answered by divine creation. Alusi and Tabatabai dispute that this was asked."}, {"id": "17:85/q04/p3", "position": "They asked about the Quran's form, source, arrangement, or why revelation came to Muhammad.", "reasons": "Jishumi lists composition and bearer; Razi says the question could contrast divine revelation with poetry or soothsaying; Islahi says the concealed complaint concerned God's choice of recipient."}, {"id": "17:85/q04/p4", "position": "They asked how a soul from God can be punished in a body.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas reports the Jewish question; the answer came through Gabriel, whom the Jews then called their enemy, prompting 2:97."}, {"id": "17:85/q04/p5", "position": "They asked about Gabriel's attributes and descent with revelation.", "reasons": "Jishumi attributes this to Ibn Abbas; Alusi reports Hasan and Qatada asking how Gabriel came and delivered revelation."}, {"id": "17:85/q04/p6", "position": "They asked about Jesus.", "reasons": "Nahhas says the reply counters the Christian claim about him."}]}
{"id": "17:85/q05", "question": "How is the hamza in 'they ask you' pronounced?", "turns_on": "The reading changes pronunciation but not meaning.", "positions": [{"id": "17:85/q05/p1", "position": "Some readers fully pronounce the hamza, while Hafs eases it.", "reasons": "Qiraat-ER says the semantic value remains the same."}]}
{"id": "17:85/q06", "question": "How does asking with ʿan work here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "17:85/q06/p1", "position": "An information-seeking verb may take its second object directly or with ʿan, more often with ʿan.", "reasons": "Al-Raghib gives this verse as the example, as cited by Itqan."}]}
{"id": "17:85/q07", "question": "What does the Arabic word rūḥ mean and how is it formed?", "turns_on": "The sources relate it to wind, breath, movement, life, and other Quranic uses.", "positions": [{"id": "17:85/q07/p1", "position": "It can name the soul or life-principle of a body.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba notes God takes it at death; Damghani includes animals and living beings. Ibn Jawzi links Adam; Elmalili distinguishes motive force, biological life, and conscious human life. Tabatabai states ordinary Arabic usage enables sensation and voluntary movement."}, {"id": "17:85/q07/p2", "position": "It is related to wind or breath.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba links rūḥ, rawḥ, and rīḥ through vowels and patterns, comparing other word families. Jishumi's Abu Ali explains waw becoming ya under kasra and gives arwāḥ as plural. Dhu al-Rumma's fire poem uses rūḥ for blowing; Ibn Jawzi glosses its tinder and measured breath. Mawardi and Wahidi derive the animal spirit's name from wind."}, {"id": "17:85/q07/p3", "position": "It can name Gabriel.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba cites Holy Spirit and Trustworthy Spirit in 2:253 and 26:193–194; Kuranyolu surveys usages."}, {"id": "17:85/q07/p4", "position": "It can name divine revelation or the Quran.", "reasons": "Tabatabai calls knowledge and revelation life-giving figuratively; Kuranyolu cites 16:2, 40:15, 42:52."}, {"id": "17:85/q07/p5", "position": "It can mean motion, expansion, or a motivating force.", "reasons": "Wahidi cites a broad foot, wide bowl, and wine called rāḥ; Elmalili extends the usage to forces such as electricity."}, {"id": "17:85/q07/p6", "position": "It can mean blowing or breath that revives fire.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba and Ibn Jawzi cite Dhu al-Rumma's line; the blowing is related to wind from the spirit."}]}
{"id": "17:85/q08", "question": "What is the spirit asked about here?", "turns_on": "Sources use context and other Quranic occurrences to choose among human spirit, Gabriel, Quran, angel, distinct creature, and Jesus.", "positions": [{"id": "17:85/q08/p1", "position": "The animating human or animal spirit.", "reasons": "Wahidi Basit says this is the immediate sense; Ibn Atiyya, Razi, Abu Hayyan, Alusi, and most exegetes prefer it. Razi links the previous verse's discussion of each person's pattern; al-Dimashqi cautions against importing other Quranic uses. The question includes how it animates and enters the body."}, {"id": "17:85/q08/p2", "position": "A mighty angel distinct from Gabriel.", "reasons": "Muqatil describes a human-faced guardian of angels, surpassed only by the Throne. Ali's report gives seventy thousand faces and tongues whose praises generate angels; other reports give ten or eleven thousand wings or a hundred thousand heads. Ibn Atiyya, Razi, Ibn Kathir, Abu Hayyan, Alusi, and Tabatabai question reports or the angel identification."}, {"id": "17:85/q08/p3", "position": "The Quran or revelation.", "reasons": "Hasan and others cite 42:52, 16:2, and 40:15; it revives hearts and is divine speech, not Muhammad's. Jishumi, Razi, Tabrisi, Asad, and Islahi use the surrounding Quran discussion. Tabatabai argues Gabriel descends with a distinct Spirit bearing the Quran and rejects the contextual inference. Tabatabai reports the Quran identification as figurative life-giving speech."}, {"id": "17:85/q08/p4", "position": "Gab

riel.", "reasons": "Qatada, Hasan, and Ibn Abbas are cited; 26:193 calls him the Trustworthy Spirit, 19:17 God's Spirit, and 19:64 says he descends by God's command. Tabatabai objects that being called spirit elsewhere cannot make every occurrence Gabriel, since Jesus too is called spirit. Abdurrazzaq adds Ibn Abbas's image of five hundred years' bird flight between Gabriel's shoulders."}, {"id": "17:85/q08/p5", "position": "A human-shaped created kind or host distinct from humans and sometimes angels.", "reasons": "Mujahid describes heads, limbs and eating; Ibn Abbas says such a being accompanies each descending angel; Abu Salih calls it human-shaped but nonhuman. Salman places Spirit above angels yet below cherubim. Other reports say angels cannot see them."}, {"id": "17:85/q08/p6", "position": "Its particular identity is left unspecified.", "reasons": "Qurtubi favors God's deliberate withholding; Tabari and Ibn Kathir describe it as a matter God alone knows, without identifying one creature. Qurtubi says the humility of not knowing one's own self points to still less grasp of the Creator."}, {"id": "17:85/q08/p7", "position": "Jesus.", "reasons": "Mawardi says this denies both Christian sonship and Jewish slander; Nahhas similarly frames the question against Christian claims. Tabatabai notes Jesus as a created word and spirit through 'Be' without ordinary procreation."}, {"id": "17:85/q08/p8", "position": "A distinct being or life-bestowing reality of the divine command order.", "reasons": "Tabatabai separates Spirit from angels in 78:38 and 97:4, connects it to all levels of life and prophetic support, and cites reports of a being greater than Gabriel accompanying Muhammad and the Imams. Qashani locates it in immaterial command."}]}
{"id": "17:85/q09", "question": "What is the human spirit or self in its nature?", "turns_on": "Views differ on whether the self is a body, a subtle body, an accident of life, or an immaterial substance.", "positions": [{"id": "17:85/q09/p1", "position": "A simple, immaterial substance governs and survives the body.", "reasons": "Razi argues that identity persists as body parts change or vanish; self-awareness remains without awareness of organs; calling them 'my' organs distinguishes owner and owned; one subject perceives, desires, speaks and acts through different organs; knowledge persists without sense organs; thinking and asceticism strengthen soul while weakening body; accumulated intelligibles do not displace one another; bodily transformations and angelic appearances separate form from essence; martyrs, the dead, and the tranquil soul survive bodily death in 3:169, 40:46, 71:25, 89:27–28, 6:61–62; dreams and practices for the dead corroborate survival; 59:19, 6:93, 23:12–14, 15:29, 91:7–8, and 76:2 distinguish spirit from bodily fashioning and responsibility. He locates its initial influence at the heart, rejects bodily and accident theories, and answers objections from divine likeness, bodily Quranic wording, and martyrs' provision. Ibn Sina's self-awareness and philosophers' survival support the view; Alusi favors an immaterial cognizer given when a prepared body needs governance but regards scriptural proof as suggestive rather than decisive. Razi eliminates pure elements and dense organs and knows no theory of a human body outside the body. Alusi notes possible differences between human and spirit, reports Ibn al-Qayyim's image-based individuation and rebuts an immaterialist difficulty, and says spirit may illuminate scattered original bodily parts. Elmalili describes spirit as shaping disposition toward guidance or error."}, {"id": "17:85/q09/p2", "position": "A subtle airy body flows through an animal's passages or members.", "reasons": "Jishumi's teachers, Tabrisī's theologians and al-Murtada, Biqai's Sunni preference, Ibn Kathir's al-Suhayli, and others use airflow or water in a tree or rosewater in a rose. Ali ibn Isa says life is in every part. Nasafi rejects the fine-air definition. Ibn Kathir says al-Suhayli's account of one thing called spirit and soul by aspect is good."}, {"id": "17:85/q09/p3", "position": "Its precise anatomy or essence remains unknown.", "reasons": "Wahidi reports brain, blood, and whole-body locations, citing 14:17 for the last, but calls them speculation; Baydawi and Bursevi say sense-based knowing reaches attributes rather than essence. Kuranyolu says science has not established the soul's nature."}, {"id": "17:85/q09/p4", "position": "The spirit is in the heart, as a meaning or indivisible occupant.", "reasons": "Jishumi and Tabrisī report a meaning in the heart; Razi reports a heart location and argues free choice and knowledge reside there, citing 7:179, 58:22, 26:193–194."}, {"id": "17:85/q09/p5", "position": "The human is the visible body, bodily structure, or its elemental mixture.", "reasons": "Razi cites most theologians, physicians, deniers of survival, Abu al-Husayn al-Basri, and early Mutazilites; they variously specify shape, temperament, or bodies bearing life and power. Razi rejects this through identity, unity of subject, bodily change, and survival arguments; he says a human-shaped angel and a transformed person refute shape as definition."}, {"id": "17:85/q09/p6", "position": "The spirit is the living human person.", "reasons": "Al-Ikhshid and al-Nazzam identify it with the morally responsible human; Shawkani calls it the essential self, but these formulations vary in whether they mean body or distinct self."}, {"id": "17:85/q09/p7", "position": "The spirit is blood.", "reasons": "Wahidi and Razi report the inference from blood loss causing death."}, {"id": "17:85/q09/p8", "position": "The spirit is inhaled air or bodily vapor.", "reasons": "Wahidi cites strangulation; Razi reports airy spirits mixed with innate heat generated in heart or brain; Farghani describes a life-bearing vapor from the heart."}, {"id": "17:85/q09/p9", "position": "A luminous celestial body permeates the prepared human body.", "reasons": "Razi calls this worthy of reflection; investigators and Ibn al-Qayyim call it strong and claim scripture, Sunna, consensus, reason, nature, and 105 proofs. Thabit ibn Qurra links the soul to such bodies; Alusi allows his composite version."}, {"id": "17:85/q09/p10", "position": "Spirit is the accident or quality of life.", "reasons": "Abu al-Hudhayl identifies it with life; Mufid, Balkhi and Baghdad Mutazilites define life as the accident allowing power, knowledge and choice. Razi says a human who knows and acts is a substance, not an accident; Alusi rejects postmortem nonexistence on this basis."}, {"id": "17:85/q09/p11", "position": "The spirit is an indivisible part of the brain.", "reasons": "Razi reports this as an alternative to the heart location; Alusi lists it among many definitions."}, {"id": "17:85/q09/p12", "position": "The spirit is innate fiery heat.", "reasons": "Razi reports a view combining heat with cardiac and cerebral spirits; Alusi lists the same."}, {"id": "17:85/q09/p13", "position": "Humanity is the union of body and a distinct soul.", "reasons": "Razi says the union ends at death while the soul persists."}]}
{"id": "17:85/q10", "question": "Are spirit and soul the same thing?", "turns_on": "Reports use the terms interchangeably, distinguish them, or say usage determines their relation.", "positions": [{"id": "17:85/q10/p1", "position": "They are one in essence or are used interchangeably.", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd says most scholars and reports exchange the words; Abu Hurayra's death report uses soul and spirit for one departure and ascent. Ibn al-Qayyim follows the majority; al-Suhayli says one thing has different aspects."}, {"id": "17:85/q10/p2", "position": "The terms coincide in some uses and differ in others.", "reasons": "Alusi concludes contextual usage decides; Elmalili notes the identity question remains disputed."}, {"id": "17:85/q10/p3", "position": "They are distinct entities or levels.", "reasons": "Ibn Habib makes spirit breath and soul the feeling form that leaves in sleep; Ibn Mandah reports earthy-fiery versus luminous, or human versus divine; hadith scholars contrast worldly desire with afterlife orientation; Farghani makes soul vapor shaped by spiritual spirit; Ibn Barjan makes spirit from soul's inner reality. Sufis say discipline may turn soul into spirit."}, {"id": "17:85/q10/p4", "position": "There is no demonstrated answer on whether they are one or two.", "reasons": "Ibn Jawzi rejects unproved medical and philosophical theories and cites early Muslims' restraint."}]}
{"id": "17:85/q11", "question": "When did spirits come into being relative to bodies?", "turns_on": "Some put spirits before bodies; others at bodily formation, and an ancient view treats them as eternal.", "positions": [{"id": "17:85/q11/p1", "position": "They arise with or after bodily formation.", "reasons": "Ghazali, Aristotle, and Ibn al-Qayyim are cited. Ibn al-Qayyim uses the fetal hadith: an angel breathes spirit after four months; if it existed earlier, the report would say bring and insert. Alusi favors an immaterial cognizer bestowed when bodily temperament becomes ready, and cites 23:14."}, {"id": "17:85/q11/p2", "position": "They were created before bodies.", "reasons": "Sulami's Ibn Ata and Wasiti report prior creation, and one report makes Muhammad's spirit first. Al-Khattabi reads the 'gathered troops' hadith this way; Ibn Hazm posits a separate barzakh, though Alusi rejects his claim of consensus and says no scriptural proof establishes it. Ibn al-Qayyim criticizes a two-thousand-year report's chain."}, {"id": "17:85/q11/p3", "position": "The soul or spirit is eternal.", "reasons": "Alusi attributes this to Plato and predecessors, while saying Muslims agree on origination; he reports a later attempt to reinterpret Plato subtly."}]}
{"id": "17:85/q12", "question": "Does the spirit die when the body dies?", "turns_on": "Death may mean annihilation, bodily separation, or a changed mod

e of life.", "positions": [{"id": "17:85/q12/p1", "position": "It survives the body's death and continues reward or punishment.", "reasons": "Alusi reports philosophers' reasoning: the body neither causes nor sustains the immaterial soul, and its loss need not destroy it; body is an instrument and initial condition, not a continuing cause. Martyrs' and other spirits are rewarded; Alusi notes annihilation remains possible in his theology even if it does not occur."}, {"id": "17:85/q12/p2", "position": "It dies or ceases.", "reasons": "Alusi reports arguments from every soul tasting death, the angels' death, and the two deaths in 40:11. Some say animal spirits cease if animals are not resurrected; others call the spirit a life accident ending at death, which Alusi rejects."}, {"id": "17:85/q12/p3", "position": "Its death is separation from the body, not annihilation.", "reasons": "Alusi says shock of the trumpet need not mean death, destruction can mean loss of function, and 40:11 does not prove a second annihilation; the spirit returns for lasting reward or punishment. For animal spirits he makes survival conditional on resurrection."}]}
{"id": "17:85/q13", "question": "Where are spirits after bodily death?", "turns_on": "Reports propose Paradise, graves, lower heaven, Sijjin, varied abodes, or free movement.", "positions": [{"id": "17:85/q13/p1", "position": "Their abodes differ by rank and state.", "reasons": "Investigators place prophets in highest Illiyyin, martyrs in Paradise, and children in blessed places; the Prophet's last prayer asks for the highest companion. Nasafi gives four believer ranks and Sijjin for unbelievers. Al-Ifsah, Qurtubi, and Suyuti reconcile varied images and movements; Alusi rejects Nasafi's denial that obedient believers enjoy Paradise. Ibn Rajab says the report of return to earth cannot override many Paradise reports and 20:55 concerns bodies."}, {"id": "17:85/q13/p2", "position": "Martyrs' spirits dwell in green birds; other souls may also take bird forms.", "reasons": "Ibn Masud's Muslim report describes green birds; variants mention green or white birds and sparrows for believers' children. Al-Kurani calls these fitting imaginal bodies. Ibn al-Mubarak's Ka'b report places martyrs by a river under a green dome. Alusi answers the objection that two spirits cannot be in one bird by saying the bird may have only the martyr's spirit or contain it as a fetus is contained."}, {"id": "17:85/q13/p3", "position": "Believers' spirits gather in a heavenly house.", "reasons": "Wahb places a white house in the seventh heaven."}, {"id": "17:85/q13/p4", "position": "Unbelievers' spirits inhabit black birds in Hell.", "reasons": "Umm Bishr reports black birds eating and drinking fire; Nasafi places them in Sijjin beneath the seventh earth while connected to their bodies."}, {"id": "17:85/q13/p5", "position": "Spirits reside in grave courtyards.", "reasons": "Ibn Hazm attributes this to most hadith scholars; Ibn Abd al-Barr favors it except for martyrs; Mujahid says spirits remain above graves seven days. Alusi accepts temporary visits, not permanent confinement; greetings and shown seats can be mediated by a connection."}, {"id": "17:85/q13/p6", "position": "All spirits stay in the lowest heaven near Adam.", "reasons": "A group uses the Mi'raj sight of people at Adam's right and left; Alusi replies that being seen there need not mean residence."}, {"id": "17:85/q13/p7", "position": "A spirit can move, visit, converse, and meet living spirits in dreams.", "reasons": "Malik is cited for release to go where it wishes, though Alusi limits that if sound. Other investigators propose rapid travel or a nonlocal connection. Alusi says dreams can carry meetings but cannot alone establish legal rulings; he cites Thabit's dream about armor, debt and emancipation and Ibn al-Qayyim's parallels. Some debts may detain spirits."}, {"id": "17:85/q13/p8", "position": "The soul remains below while a distinct spirit rises.", "reasons": "Ibn Barjan uses this to explain Moses at his grave and Abraham in heaven; an evildoer's soul is cast down. Alusi says it reconciles seemingly conflicting reports."}, {"id": "17:85/q13/p9", "position": "An immaterial spirit has no spatial abode.", "reasons": "Alusi says only the body it governs is located; he nonetheless allows connection and perception in various places."}]}
{"id": "17:85/q14", "question": "Can one spirit govern more than one body?", "turns_on": "Sufi accounts allow multiple manifestations; philosophers challenge shared knowledge.", "positions": [{"id": "17:85/q14/p1", "position": "Yes, an original body and imaginal or extraordinary manifestation can share a spirit.", "reasons": "Sufis compare Gabriel appearing as Dihya without leaving the Lote Tree and Quran as a pale man; Alusi says the shared-knowledge objection proves too little."}, {"id": "17:85/q14/p2", "position": "No, one soul in several bodies would give them identical knowledge.", "reasons": "Alusi reports philosophers' objection and replies that the inference from different knowledge is too weak."}]}
{"id": "17:85/q15", "question": "What inward account of spirit and spiritual growth is given?", "turns_on": "Mystical notes describe several distinct aspects of spirit, embodiment, divine disclosure, and disciplined ascent.", "positions": [{"id": "17:85/q15/p1", "position": "Spirit is a subtle created light or reality whose effects animate bodies and open unseen perception.", "reasons": "Sulami reports a ray of reality, a delicacy drawn toward divine knowledge, and spirits predating bodies or emerging from divine beauty and holiness; Abu Said al-Haddad links life, intellect, covenant, and accountability, while Ibn Ata describes the spirit as pure and bright, unveiling the unseen. Wasiti says spirits were created and seized before bodies."}, {"id": "17:85/q15/p2", "position": "The seeker ascends by discipline from outward practice through purification, illumination, and self-effacement.", "reasons": "Bursevi's Najmiyyah gives heart, secret, spirit, hidden and witnessing stages. Alusi lists four stages, then details repentance, ascetic audit, retreat and remembrance, unveiling, tranquility, annihilation, and sober return. He rejects literal transfer of divine attributes into human soul; a saint's motive for jihad may conceal a wish to escape worship."}, {"id": "17:85/q15/p3", "position": "Spirit is worship, while only God sustains existence.", "reasons": "Sulami reports this twice, once from Baghdadi voices, emphasizing God's care and preservation."}, {"id": "17:85/q15/p4", "position": "Spirits experience divine disclosure, concealment, love, and varying nourishment.", "reasons": "Sulami says disclosure brings bliss and concealment suffering; Wasiti lists love, fear, hope and truthfulness, with gnosis grounded in God's knowledge. Favors may make spirits forget; prophetic spirits feed on subtle address, righteous spirits on regard, and ordinary spirits on food. A poem imagines ascent beyond stars."}, {"id": "17:85/q15/p5", "position": "Spirit's presence gives the body's limbs light and proper conduct.", "reasons": "Sulami says its meeting illumines and adorns bodies; veiling causes improper action; some spirits turn from created things through witnessing the Real and receive the name peace."}, {"id": "17:85/q15/p6", "position": "Two spirits serve death and ordinary life.", "reasons": "Abu Said al-Qurashi distinguishes departure that ends life from breath enabling eating and drinking."}, {"id": "17:85/q15/p7", "position": "All spirits descend from the Prophet's primordial spirit.", "reasons": "Bursevi's Najmiyyah reads the spirit breathed into Adam and Jesus as deriving from Muhammad's spirit, and connects Adam's descendants and the Prophet's banner."}]}
{"id": "17:85/q16", "question": "Why repeat 'the spirit' in the answer?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "17:85/q16/p1", "position": "The noun is repeated for emphasis and special concern.", "reasons": "Alusi notes the answer could have used a pronoun."}]}
{"id": "17:85/q17", "question": "What does 'from my Lord's command' mean?", "turns_on": "Amr is read as a matter known to God, His act of creating, a direct immaterial order, revelation, or sovereign power.", "positions": [{"id": "17:85/q17/p1", "position": "Spirit is a matter whose reality belongs to God's exclusive knowledge.", "reasons": "Farra and Tabari read amr as divine knowledge; Wahidi says no servant has this account, and Bursevi takes the possessive as exclusive knowledge. Alusi reads min as partitive or explanatory with amr as affair, and says the phrase honors the spirit and Lord. Ibn Ashur calls it a genus-level redirection, not a physical description."}, {"id": "17:85/q17/p2", "position": "It is God's act or creative command: spirit is originated by Him.", "reasons": "Razi cites amr as act in 11:97 and 11:66 and change from ignorance to knowledge as proof of origination; Abu Hayyan likewise cites 11:97. Baydawi and Alusi explain 'Be' without matter or organs; Jishumi argues what can be withdrawn cannot be eternal. Ibn Ashur takes min as origin.
